study.title: 1 Corinthians 11 - Order in worship, memory of the Supper and personal examination
study.overview: In this chapter, Paul corrects two types of disorder in the church of Corinth: the lack of reverence and discernment in public worship, first in the way men and women presented themselves in prayer and prophecy, and then in the way the church celebrated the Lord's Supper. The apostle deals not only with external appearance, but of spiritual posture, respect for God's command, consideration for the community and fidelity to the sense of the Supper. The chapter unites apostolic authority, tradition received from Christ, communion and spiritual discipline.

outline.title: Order, honor and discernment in public prayer
outline.explanation: Paul calls the church to imitate his example in that he imitates Christ, and then guides on the relationship between man, woman and head, that is, authority and honor. The central point is that public worship should not communicate dishonor, rebellion or confusion, but reflect the recognized order in the churches.

outline.title: Rebuke divisions and selfishness at the Supper
outline.explanation: Paul ceases to praise and proceeds to censor the church because his meetings were dealing more damage than well. The Supper, which should express unity and mutual care, had become an opportunity for division, humiliation of the poor and unworthy behavior.

outline.title: The institution of the Supper and its meaning
outline.explanation: The apostle transmits what he has received from the Lord: the bread and the cup as signs connected to the body and blood of Christ, given in remembrance of him. Each celebration announces the death of the Lord and points to his coming.

outline.title: Discernment, judgment and self-correction
outline.explanation: Whoever participates in an unworthy way becomes guilty, because he does not correctly discern the body of the Lord. Therefore Paul orsor personal examination, practical repentance, mutual waiting and the solution of hunger at home, so that the meeting of the church will not become an occasion for judgment.

study.context: The chapter shows a royal church, with spiritual gifts, but also with practical tensions in worship. The notes indicate that Paul is correcting concrete abuses in the public worship and the Lord's Supper. Tyndale notes that the teachings transmitted in 11:2 belong to a Christian tradition received and passed on; Matthew Henry points out that Paul faces serious disorders in the assembly and at the Lord's table; Adam Clarke emphasizes that the chapter deals with irregularities in worship, divisions and the celebration of the Supper. The text itself suggests that Paul writes with pastoral authority to reform existing abuses.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that Christian freedom does not eliminate order, reverence and responsibility. In 11:1, Paul presents his example as a model only because his life is subject to Christ; apostolic imitation is never autonomous. In 11:3-16, the discussion of head, honor and coverage points to an orderly view of relations in worship, without denying the shared dignity between man and woman, for the text also states that in the Lord none is independent of the other (11:11-12). In 11:17-22, the church is guilty of transforming fellowship into selfishness, showing that worship can be corrupted when the strong despise the weak. In 11:23-26, the Supper is presented as a tradition received from the Lord and as a proclaiming memorial: it proclaims the death of Christ until its return. In 11:27-32, participating unworthily is not mere ritual error, but lack of spiritual discernment; therefore the examination of oneself is necessary. The judgment of the Lord here is disciplinary and corrective, in order to avoid the final condemnation with the world. In 11:33-34, the pastoral solution is simple and concrete: to wait for each other and to treat the common hunger outside the holy moment of the table.

scholarViews.insight: In 11:2, Paul's instructions are understood as an authoritative Christian tradition, received and delivered orally, not as personal opinion.
In 11:17, Paul proceeds to rebuke with serious disorders in the church, showing that he approves what he can, but condemns what is scandalous.
In 11:34, guidance is not to turn the church's meeting into a common meal; those who hunger must eat at home, to avoid judgment on the assembly.

questions: What attitudes of mine, in the worship and coexistence of the church, communicate honor to Christ and consideration for the brethren?
When I participate in the Lord's Supper, am I discerning the spiritual significance of the body and blood of Christ, or just by fulfilling a rite?
How can I practice personal examination, reconciliation and wait for others before I approach the Lord's table?
study.practice: Before the next meeting of the church, take an honest examination of your attitude: if there is pride, haste, contempt or division, confess this to God and seek reconciliation. As you participate in the Supper, consciously remember the death of the Lord and his return, and decide to treat the brothers with greater care. If there is a common physical need, take care of it outside the moment of worship, not to mix distraction and reverence.
study.uncertainty: The text and notes do not allow to define with absolute certainty all the cultural details of the head cover at 11:3-16, nor accurately fix the range of expressions such as 'because of angels' and 'the nature'. The notes provided suggest historical and pastoral readings, but do not authorize to affirm more than that. It is also not possible to determine, only with the notes given, all the specific customs of the Corinthian community meal beyond what the chapter describes.
